section_summary: This section contains three successive monthly political and economic reports on Japan for March, April, and May 1936, transmitted by U.S. Ambassador Joseph C. Grew to the Secretary of State. The reports chronicle the domestic and international repercussions of the February 26 Incident, including the collapse of the Okada Cabinet, the establishment of the Hirota Cabinet under military pressure, extensive Army purges, and trials of implicated officers. In foreign relations, they document rising friction and border clashes with the Soviet Union, Japanese expansionism and rampant smuggling in North China, and bilateral tensions with the United States regarding oil storage mandates, automotive manufacturing restrictions, and cotton textile tariffs.

subfiles.about: Monthly report detailing Japanese political, military, economic, and diplomatic conditions during March 1936 in the immediate aftermath of the February 26 Incident.
subfiles.summary: This report covers the stabilization of Tokyo under martial law following the suppression of the February 26 military insurrection and details the installation of the Hirota Cabinet after Army leaders rejected moderate nominees. It outlines the four major Army demands accepted by Prime Minister Koki Hirota, the resignation of senior Supreme War Council generals, the reshuffle of military staff posts, and the suspended court-martial of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa. In external affairs, the document assesses border tensions with Soviet forces, negotiations over North China, the replacement of Kwantung Army Commander Jiro Minami by Kenkichi Ueda, relations with Great Britain and Siam, and the deportation of British journalist Gerald Sampson. It concludes with an analysis of government bond policy under Finance Minister Eiichi Baba, general economic conditions, and complete schedules of despatches and telegrams sent to Washington during March 1936.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of March, 1936 (Report No. 114)

subfiles.about: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits Report No. 115 reviewing internal political affairs, foreign relations, and economic conditions in Japan during April 1936.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits the Embassy's monthly report for April 1936, which details the formal appointment of Hachiro Arita as Foreign Minister and the replacement of Vice Minister Mamoru Shigemitsu by Kensuke Horinouchi. The report examines relations with the United States concerning petroleum storage laws, Japanese land leases in Davao, and goodwill visits by Philippine assemblymen and American Veterans of Foreign Wars. In foreign affairs, it notes Soviet-Japanese border skirmishes near Suifenho and Huilin, negotiations with China, the German Economic Mission's trade arrangement for Manchurian soya beans, and trade disputes with Australia over rayon and wool. Domestically, it discusses War Minister Juichi Terauchi's efforts to enforce discipline, political party alignments, bond conversion operations by Finance Minister Baba, and incorporates monthly lists of despatches and telegrams forwarded to the Department.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. P.R. 101 Transmitting Report on Conditions in Japan for April, 1936 (Report No. 115)

subfiles.about: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits Report No. 116 reviewing political developments, foreign relations, and trade friction in Japan during May 1936.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits the monthly report for May 1936, addressing rising economic and diplomatic friction between Japan and Western powers. It examines Japanese reactions to increased United States tariffs on cotton textiles, diplomatic protests by the United States and Great Britain regarding widespread illicit smuggling operations in East Hopei, and the Diet's enactment of the Automobile Industry Control Law restricting foreign assemblers. The report recounts negotiations between foreign oil corporations and the Mitsui firm to satisfy mandatory storage regulations, discussions on the Davao land tenure controversy, and the official Tokyo visit of Admiral Orin G. Murfin on the USS Augusta. In continental affairs, it records sharp Chinese government protests over East Hopei contraband operations and the War Office's formal decision to substantially reinforce the Japanese garrison in North China.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. P.R. 102 Transmitting Report on Conditions in Japan for May, 1936 (Report No. 116)
